info.name: Atlas API (v0.0.0)
info.description: Atlas authentication & user management API. Generated from the code-derived OpenAPI document (the same one served at /v1/openapi.json) by scripts/gen-postman.mjs. Import this collection, import the environment template, set `baseUrl` and your keys, and every request is pre-wired with auth, path/query params, and a body example.

item.name: POST Decide for the principal an access token stands for. The token is verified first (an active Atlas session token, or

request.description:
Decide for the principal an access token stands for. The token is verified first (an active Atlas session token, or a token from a trusted issuer); its claims map to the principal and parents per the token mapping. An invalid token is a 401, not a deny.
**Required scope:** `abac:evaluate`

`POST /v1/abac/authorize_token`

item.name: POST List the resources of a type a principal may perform an action on, paged (`limit`, `starting_after`; the response c

request.description:
List the resources of a type a principal may perform an action on, paged (`limit`, `starting_after`; the response carries `has_more` and `next_cursor`). Candidates are the Atlas resources of that type (their metadata are the attributes) or the `candidates` you send. The policies are reduced to one filter and applied to every candidate; `method` says whether that worked or each candidate was evaluated in full.
**Required scope:** `abac:evaluate`

`POST /v1/abac/accessible_resources`

item.name: POST Partial evaluation (data filtering): ask what is left of the decision when an entity is unknown. With a known princ

request.description:
Partial evaluation (data filtering): ask what is left of the decision when an entity is unknown. With a known principal, an action and a resource TYPE, the response is a residual `filter` over the resource attributes (or constant `true`/`false`) that is equivalent to evaluating the policies on each resource. `unknowns: ["principal"]` answers "who may do this on that resource". Relationship conditions (`fga.check`) are resolved to id lists from the policy’s FGA store unless `resolve_relations` is false. `output` asks for a ready-made parameterised SQL WHERE (`sql`: dialect and a field-to-column map) and/or a Prisma where object (`prisma`: a field map). Policies that build sets from unknown attributes cannot be expressed as a filter and are refused with a message naming the policy.
**Required scope:** `abac:evaluate`

`POST /v1/abac/partial_evaluate`

item.name: POST Policy decision point: ask whether `principal` may perform `action` on `resource` given `context` (and optional ext

request.description:
Policy decision point: ask whether `principal` may perform `action` on `resource` given `context` (and optional extra `entities` for hierarchy). All enabled policies are evaluated together with Cedar semantics: a matching forbid wins, otherwise a matching permit allows, otherwise deny. Each decision is written to the event feed (type authz.decision), so log streams carry it.
**Required scope:** `abac:evaluate`

`POST /v1/abac/evaluate`

item.name: POST Create an ABAC policy from `source` written in the Cedar-subset policy language (permit/forbid with when/unless ove

request.description:
Create an ABAC policy from `source` written in the Cedar-subset policy language (permit/forbid with when/unless over principal, action, resource and context attributes; `fga.check(...)` consults the policy’s FGA store). Source that does not parse is refused with the character position; with an entity schema set it is also type-checked and every problem is reported. Optional `tests` are saved with version 1.
**Required scope:** `abac:write`

`POST /v1/abac_policies`

item.name: POST Run test cases against a policy version (default: the current one), or against a draft `source` and `tests` sent in

request.description:
Run test cases against a policy version (default: the current one), or against a draft `source` and `tests` sent in the body, without saving anything. Each test is a request plus the expected decision; the policy is evaluated on its own, not with the rest of the set. The response also carries `coverage`: which rules and `when`/`unless` clauses the tests exercised (a clause no test saw both true and false is listed as a gap), with line numbers.
**Required scope:** `abac:read`

`POST /v1/abac_policies/{id}/test`

request.description:

item.name: PUT Set the ABAC entity schema: `entity_types` (attributes with `boolean`, `long`, `string`, `set`, `entity` and `record

request.description:
Set the ABAC entity schema: `entity_types` (attributes with `boolean`, `long`, `string`, `set`, `entity` and `record` types, `required: false` for optional ones, and `member_of`) and `actions` (`applies_to` principal and resource types and a `context`). Every problem is reported with its path. Once set, policies and templates are type-checked when saved: unknown attributes, optional attributes read without a `has` guard, wrong operand types, unknown entity types and actions, and actions that do not apply to the policy’s principal and resource types. The response lists the errors the schema would give the policies and links already stored.
**Required scope:** `abac:write`

`PUT /v1/abac_schema`

item.name: POST Create a conditional-access policy. `conditions` (applications, userIds, groups, orgs, roles, networkZones {include

request.description:
Create a conditional-access policy. `conditions` (applications, userIds, groups, orgs, roles, networkZones {include, exclude}, countries, riskLevels, deviceTrust, authMethods, timeWindow) are ANDed; an empty condition matches anything. `grants` are allow, block, require_mfa, require_acr, require_policy_acceptance or require_action. `stages` limits it to sign_in, authorize and/or token (default all). Further conditions: devicePlatforms, osVersion {min, max}, clientTypes, userAttributes, userRiskLevels, signInRiskLevels and principalIds. Further grants: require_auth_strength (mfa, passwordless, phishing_resistant), require_device_bound_session, require_password_change, sign_in_frequency, max_session_age and persistent_session. `mode: report_only` logs `access_policy.would_block` and never denies. `targets` picks user, machine and/or agent principals (default user). A matching block wins; step-up grants are unioned.
**Required scope:** `access_policies:write`

`POST /v1/access_policies`

item.name: POST Impact preview: replay a draft policy (`draft`: conditions, grants, stages, targets) against the sampled sign-ins o

request.description:
Impact preview: replay a draft policy (`draft`: conditions, grants, stages, targets) against the sampled sign-ins of the last `days` (1-30, default 7) and get how many would have been allowed, stepped up or blocked, plus the affected users. Nothing is stored or enforced.
**Required scope:** `access_policies:read`

`POST /v1/access_policies/impact`

item.name: POST What-if: describe a request (stage, ip, application, orgs, roles, country, risk level, device trust, auth methods,

request.description:
What-if: describe a request (stage, ip, application, orgs, roles, country, risk level, device trust, auth methods, whether MFA was verified) and see the decision, the policies that matched and the unmet step-up requirements. Pass `policy_id` to test one policy even if it is disabled.
**Required scope:** `access_policies:read`

`POST /v1/access_policies/simulate`

item.name: POST Meter usage against a key's spend caps, atomically. Body: amount (positive integer), unit (app-defined, e.g. reques

request.description:
Meter usage against a key's spend caps, atomically. Body: amount (positive integer), unit (app-defined, e.g. requests or usd_cents), optional idempotency_key. When the debit fits every cap for that unit it is recorded (day, month and total counters, plus second/minute counters for a unit capped on those windows) and allowed:true is returned; when it would exceed a cap — or is larger than a per-request cap — NOTHING is recorded and the response is 200 with allowed:false and code LIMIT_EXCEEDED, so you enforce it in your own transaction. Concurrent debits on one key serialize: two can never both pass a cap only one fits under. Second and minute windows are fixed windows aligned to the UTC clock (a 600/minute cap refuses the 601st request until the next whole minute); day and month windows are UTC calendar windows. The same idempotency_key (kept 24 hours) returns the first outcome without counting again (idempotent_replay:true); reusing it with a different unit or amount is 409 IDEMPOTENCY_CONFLICT. A revoked or expired key is 409 CONFLICT; an unknown id 404. The first time a cap fills or refuses a debit in a window, api_key.limit_reached is emitted (once per cap per window).
**Required scope:** `api_keys:write`

`POST /v1/api_keys/{id}/usage`

item.name: POST Mint a short-lived, JWKS-signed access JWT (token_use:api_key, jti) whose exp is clamped to the smallest of the req

request.description:
Mint a short-lived, JWKS-signed access JWT (token_use:api_key, jti) whose exp is clamped to the smallest of the request, the key expiry and the org ceiling; scopes + constraints are embedded so a resource verifies it OFFLINE against the instance JWKS. When the key registered a public_key, the token also carries cnf.jkt (proof-of-possession) and a resource additionally checks a holder-signed proof. Authenticate with (1) an sk_ bearer + the ak_ in the body, (2) an Authorization: Bearer ak_… that self-mints for itself, or (3) no bearer + x-publishable-key naming the instance with the ak_ in the body. A key only ever mints within its own instance. The api_keys:read scope applies ONLY to the sk_ path; the ak_ and publishable-key paths are self-scoped.
**Required scope:** `api_keys:read`

`POST /v1/api_keys/token`

item.name: POST Mint an end-user API key for a user, organization or machine (returns the ak_ secret once), OR import an existing k

request.description:
Mint an end-user API key for a user, organization or machine (returns the ak_ secret once), OR import an existing key by its SHA-256 hash (hash_algorithm "sha256" or "sha256_hex") so it verifies against the original secret. Normally authenticated with an sk_ key; a LAN/offline MACHINE may instead self-provision a key for ITSELF by presenting Authorization: Bearer <machine JWT> (token_use:m2m from /v1/machines/token) + x-publishable-key — the subject is forced to that machine and it cannot grant itself management-plane scopes. Pass public_key (an SPKI PEM) to make the key proof-of-possession: tokens minted from it carry cnf.jkt and a resource verifies a holder-signed proof OFFLINE. Pass limits (an array of { unit, amount, period } with period request|second|minute|day|month|total) to set per-key spend caps and rate limits, metered with POST /v1/api_keys/{id}/usage. Key controls: enabled (false = minted disabled), rate_limit { max, window_seconds } (per-key verify throttle), remaining (a use budget each successful verify spends), prefix (a custom secret prefix such as acme, giving acme_<id>_<secret>), and expires_in_seconds as an alternative to expires_at. The instance expiry policy (endUserApiKeys.defaultExpiresInSeconds / maxExpiresInSeconds) gives a key sent without an expiry the default lifetime and refuses one longer than the ceiling (400). Send required_scopes to require scopes the key must carry. A live key refused by its own policy answers valid:false with a code: insufficient_scope (missing_scopes), rate_limited (retry_after_ms, from the key rate_limit) or usage_exhausted (no remaining uses left). request.description:
The connection's live token for your backend. An oauth connection's token is refreshed first when it is expired or about to be (single-flight across processes, using the client that issued it and the connection's host_params). Built for sync workers: the response carries an `ETag` and `Cache-Control: private, max-age=<seconds until just before expires_at>`, so cache it until then; send `If-None-Match` and an unchanged, still-valid token answers 304 with no body and no vault read; `min_ttl_seconds` refreshes first when less than that much validity remains. A grant connection (client_credentials, jwt_bearer, github_app_installation, admin_consent) has its token minted from the credential Atlas holds instead, answered with `Cache-Control: no-store` (no ETag); pass `subject` to a jwt_bearer connection to act as that user (Google domain-wide delegation). Includes the captured handles (`metadata`, `token_response`) and any further named credentials. 402 CONNECTION_REQUIRED with `meta.reason` not_connected, needs_reauth, revoked or refresh_failed when there is no usable token. When the provider answers 401 to the token, call `POST /v1/connections/{id}/token/refresh` instead of re-reading. Rate limit: 6,000 reads per minute per secret key and 300 per minute per connection (RateLimit-* headers on every response, 429 with Retry-After beyond them). Reads are audited as connection.token_read once per connection per minute with the read count (a read that refreshed is always audited); the token itself is never logged.
**Required scope:** `connections:token`

The consumer and token secrets never leave Atlas. The URL must be https on an allowed host; a form-encoded body is part of the signature. Needs connections:sign.
**Required scope:** `connections:sign`

item.name: POST Make a provider API call server-side with this connection's credential, so the credential never reaches your code:

request.description:
Make a provider API call server-side with this connection's credential, so the credential never reaches your code: Atlas injects an api_key (header or query), bearer, basic or custom header, signs with an hmac_secret or OAuth 1.0a, or sends a minted client_credentials / jwt_bearer / GitHub App installation / admin consent token. Only https calls to the connection's allowed_hosts are made, with the verbs in allowed_methods (default GET, HEAD, POST). When the connection is not connected, or the provider rejects the credential, the answer is 402 CONNECTION_REQUIRED with `meta.reason` (not_connected or needs_reauth) and, for a user-owned OAuth connection when you pass `redirect_url`, `meta.authorize_url`. The audit log records the method, host and status only.
**Required scope:** `oauth_tokens:read`

`POST /v1/connections/{id}/relay`

item.name: POST Mint a scoped relay token: a signed credential for ONE connection that only works through POST /v1/connection_relay

request.description:
Mint a scoped relay token: a signed credential for ONE connection that only works through POST /v1/connection_relay/scoped, for the listed HTTP methods and https URL prefixes, and expires within the hour. It narrows what a caller can do with the connection without touching the stored provider token (which stays in the vault).
**Required scope:** `oauth_tokens:read`

`POST /v1/connections/{id}/scoped_tokens`

item.name: POST Read the tokens of up to 100 connections in one call (min_ttl_seconds applies to each). Each id gets its own result

request.description:
Read the tokens of up to 100 connections in one call (min_ttl_seconds applies to each). Each id gets its own result: status ok with the token, or status error with a code and reason (not_connected, needs_reauth, revoked, refresh_failed, unknown_connection), so one dead connection never fails the batch. The response is never cached. Counts once against the token-read rate limit.
**Required scope:** `connections:token`

`POST /v1/connections/tokens/batch`

item.name: POST Revoke the stored token at the provider, delete it from the vault and mark the connection revoked (connection.revok

request.description:
Revoke the stored token at the provider, delete it from the vault and mark the connection revoked (connection.revoked is sent once). The response is the connection plus what the provider said: provider_revoked is true only when it confirmed, "unsupported" when it has no revoke endpoint, false when it refused or was unreachable (provider_error says why). The local token is cleared in every case. Connect again to use it.
**Required scope:** `organizations:write`

`POST /v1/connections/{id}/revoke`

item.name: POST Rotate the credential: the body is the new credential (the same fields as PUT credentials). It becomes the current

request.description:
Rotate the credential: the body is the new credential (the same fields as PUT credentials). It becomes the current vault version; the replaced one stays valid for `overlap_seconds` (default 3600, up to 30 days): the relay falls back to it when the provider refuses the new one, and GET secret?version=previous returns it. `expires_at` sets the new credential's expiry. The secret never reaches the audit log.
**Required scope:** `organizations:write`

`POST /v1/connections/{id}/credentials/rotate`

item.name: POST Run an action on a connection: the input is validated against the action's schema, the connection's granted scopes

request.description:
Run an action on a connection: the input is validated against the action's schema, the connection's granted scopes are checked, and the call goes through the relay (host allow-list, credential, one refresh, retry on 429). `dry_run` returns the request without sending it; `all_pages` walks the action's pagination. The audit log records the action, provider and status, never the input.
**Required scope:** `oauth_tokens:read`

`POST /v1/connections/{id}/actions/{name}`

item.name: POST Start the provider authorization for this connection and return the URL to send the owner to. The tokens are stored

request.description:
Start the provider authorization for this connection and return the URL to send the owner to. The tokens are stored on the connection itself, never on a user: no external account is created, no sign-in method is added, no email is proven and no step-up is needed. `host_params` fill the provider's host templates for this connection (validated against a per-provider allowlist; 400 `host_params.<key>` otherwise). Reconnecting the same provider account updates the same connection; a different account answers 409 unless `create_if_new` is true. An owner OAuth client (`PUT /v1/connections/oauth_clients`) overrides the instance client.
**Required scope:** `organizations:write`

`POST /v1/connections/{id}/connect`

item.name: POST Subscribe to provider events. webhook: Atlas creates a verified ingress endpoint and, for providers whose API allow

request.description:
Subscribe to provider events. webhook: Atlas creates a verified ingress endpoint and, for providers whose API allows it (GitHub), registers the webhook there (filter: owner, repo); verified deliveries are forwarded to target_url. Other providers get an ingress_url to paste into the provider and need `scheme`. poll: a read-only catalog action runs on an interval and each new item becomes a `connection.trigger_fired` event.

item.name: POST Verify a provider webhook signature with the connection's secret (the endpoint's own signing secret, else the conne

request.description:
Verify a provider webhook signature with the connection's secret (the endpoint's own signing secret, else the connection's hmac_secret, else its OAuth client secret). Schemes: hubspot_v3 (needs method and url), shopify_hmac, intercom, zoom, slack_v0, calendly, stripe, generic_hmac_sha256. Constant-time comparison; a signed timestamp must be within the tolerance (5 minutes, Calendly 3); a delivery id or signature already seen on the connection answers `replayed`. Send the body exactly as received (`raw_body`, or base64 with raw_body_encoding). Zoom and Slack handshakes come back in `handshake`. Needs connections:webhook_verify.
**Required scope:** `connections:webhook_verify`

request.description:
Claim a custom domain (fapi or accounts). Returns 201 with the full custom_domain object — including its `id` (dom_…), which you pass to POST /v1/domains/{id}/verify once DNS is published — plus the CNAME `instructions` to follow (or a `note` for a platform subdomain, which is live immediately). Pass `dns: {provider: "cloudflare", api_token}` and Atlas writes the CNAME itself: it finds the zone, creates the record DNS-only (never proxied; `dns.proxied: true` is refused), waits briefly for it to resolve and verifies, so the domain can go from nothing to active in one call (`verified` in the response; otherwise call verify later). The token is stored encrypted and is never readable back (the response shows only `dns.provider` and `token_set`). An existing record that points elsewhere is not overwritten unless `dns.overwrite` is true (409 DNS_RECORD_CONFLICT); a rejected token is 422 DNS_TOKEN_REJECTED; no visible zone is 422 DNS_ZONE_NOT_FOUND.
**Required scope:** `domains:write`

request.description:
Check your setup in one call. Lists findings about configuration the server can see is broken or worth knowing — no sign-in method enabled, a social provider enabled without credentials, OAuth clients without redirect or post-logout URIs, a first-party client origin missing from allowed_origins, an allowed https origin that login readiness would fail (CORS or session cookie), sign-up that new users cannot complete, custom domains not serving yet, email or SMS sign-in without a provider, a Cookie Munch site that does not match the sign-in host, an OAuth client whose back-channel logout URI is failing (oauth_client_backchannel_failing: 3 consecutive failed deliveries, or one answered with a redirect, which Atlas never follows), a webhook endpoint whose last delivery was redirected (webhook_endpoint_redirecting), a webhook endpoint that is failing (webhook_endpoint_failing: a failure streak is running), switched off after repeated failures (webhook_endpoint_disabled: an error when it carries session or account events) or on a host that is not one of the instance origins or redirect hosts (webhook_endpoint_off_origin, unless it is marked external), a first-party client without a back-channel logout URI (oauth_client_no_backchannel_logout_uri), and the security posture group (group: security_posture — pkce_not_required, passkey_without_uv, auto_link_unverified) — each with a severity, a stable code, a plain message and the fix. A finding that does not apply to how the instance integrates (the embedded-component checks on an origin Atlas is confident signs in through the hosted redirect) is listed under suppressed with the reason, not in findings; integrations shows how each allowed origin was judged. ok is true when there are no errors. ok covers configuration; to confirm a browser can sign in on a given origin, use GET /v1/diagnostics/login_readiness?origin=… for each production origin. Every code is listed by GET /v1/instance/preflight/codes. request.description:
Update allowed origins and auth_config (a partial, validated, merged patch — not a replace). Open or public-suffix wildcard origins refused (a single-label https://*.your-domain.com is accepted; shared hosts like *.vercel.app on development instances only); an invalid auth_config returns 422. A method that needs email (email code, email link, password sign-up that verifies by email) is accepted even when the instance has no email provider yet (email is bring-your-own; Terraform or config import may add the provider later in the same apply): the response lists it under inactive_methods, users are not offered it, and it becomes active on its own once a provider is configured (PUT /v1/messaging_providers/email). Captcha always runs on your own provider keys: turning a captcha ON for a flow (or changing its provider) before both the provider site key (auth_config.captcha.siteKey) and its secret (PUT /v1/instance/captcha_secret) are set returns 422 CAPTCHA_KEYS_REQUIRED with param naming the missing one — store the secret first, then enable. Removing the site key while a flow uses it returns 409 CAPTCHA_IN_USE unless force=true, which also turns the captcha off on those flows. Setting the retired raw branding fields (branding.customCss / customHtmlHeader / customHtmlFooter) returns 422 naming the field — use the design settings (PUT /v1/instance/design) instead; clearing them (null or "") is accepted. The response echoes auth_config_resolved so you can confirm the change took effect, and `warnings`: an origin_still_referenced entry for every removed origin that webhook endpoints (not marked external) or OAuth client URIs still point at, naming each one and the POST /v1/instance/move_origin call that moves them. Strict writes: auth_config.strictRequestBodies (true on instances created from 2026-10 on) refuses unknown body fields with 422 UNKNOWN_FIELD on every Backend API write; set it to opt in or out, or send Atlas-Strict: true | false on one request. Every auth_config key is checked at every depth against the auth_config schema: strict, an unknown or moved key is 422 UNKNOWN_FIELD with param naming its full path (auth_config.strategies.atlasId), meta.did_you_mean when a real key is close, and meta.hint naming the endpoint for a setting that has its own (auth_config.branding → PATCH /v1/branding, design → PUT /v1/instance/design, hostedPages → PATCH /v1/instance/hosted_pages, …); lenient, the key is dropped (never stored) and listed in warnings as unknown_field and in the Atlas-Unknown-Fields header. A null on any key and an unchanged echo of a stored section (the raw auth_config GET returns, sent back as is) are always accepted.
**Required scope:** `instance:write`

`PATCH /v1/instance`

query.description: true = skip the signed test call that enabling or re-pointing the hook otherwise makes first.

request.description:
Update the before_user_create hook. Only the fields you send change; null clears. The hook is called (signed like a webhook) after the user id is assigned and before user.created, the referral call and any session. It may answer {external_id, public_metadata, private_metadata, unsafe_metadata}, or deny the sign-up with {"deny": true, "reason": "..."} or HTTP 403: the person gets 403 SIGN_UP_DENIED with your reason, no user is kept and no user.created is sent. A slow or failing hook does not block the sign-up unless fail_closed is true. The body carries data.user, data.strategy, data.referral, data.request ({client_id, app_context, login_hint} of the authorize request, nulls when absent) and data.invitation (the pending instance invitation for the address, or null) and data.organization ({id, external_id, role, role_mapped, via: sso | domain} when the sign-up comes through an organization SSO connection or a captured auto-join domain, else null). Turning the hook on, or changing the url or signing_secret of a fail_closed enabled one (or turning fail_closed on for it), first sends the signed test call: unless it returns a valid answer (an answer object, possibly empty, or a deny) the change is refused with 409 HOOK_TEST_FAILED (meta: url, status, the first 200 bytes of the response body, outcome) and the hook stays as it was. ?force=true (or force in the body) skips the test and is audit-logged. A dry run (?dry_run=true) makes the same test call and reports would_return_status 409 (or 200) without changing anything. An enabled hook that is not fail_closed is not re-tested when its url or secret changes.

Managed email: Atlas sets up your sending domain (the domain of `from_address`) on YOUR OWN Resend or Brevo account, with your API key, and sends through it once the domain is verified. Pass `transport` ("resend" | "brevo") with `config.api_key`, or `provider_id` of your configured Resend or Brevo email provider; without either the call is refused with 422 (param `config.api_key`). The key is stored, write-only, as the instance's email provider in `managed_domain` mode. Returns 201 with the DNS `records` to publish (DKIM, SPF / return-path for Resend; ownership, DKIM, DMARC for Brevo). Until the domain is verified email delivery stays unavailable and preflight warns `managed_email_unverified`. Pass `dns: {provider: "cloudflare", api_token}` and Atlas writes the records itself (DNS-only; the token is write-only) IN THE BACKGROUND: the call answers 202 at once with the records and `dns.status: "pending"`, then Atlas writes them and checks with your provider until the domain is verified (`dns.status` pending → verifying → verified; `dns.last_error` and `failed` when it cannot). No further call is needed; GET shows progress and POST …/verify checks at once. Atlas also registers a bounce / complaint webhook on your Resend or Brevo account, for this instance only (`feedback_webhook`, `feedback_webhook_id`); the counts appear in `usage`. No Atlas sending limits apply (`limits: null`): the account and its limits are yours. Atlas never uses an email account of its own. 409 when the domain is set up on another Atlas instance; 502 MANAGED_EMAIL_PROVIDER_ERROR when your provider refuses.
**Required scope:** `messaging:write`

`POST /v1/messaging_providers/email/managed`

item.name: POST Put your OWN email provider in development mode, so a development instance can send sign-in email without a verifie

request.description:
Put your OWN email provider in development mode, so a development instance can send sign-in email without a verified domain: Resend's `onboarding@resend.dev` (the default From for Resend; Resend delivers it only to your Resend account's own address), or a single sender address your provider has verified (Brevo, SES, SMTP, a Mailgun sandbox). Body: `provider_id` of your configured email provider, or `transport` + `config` (+ `from_address`) exactly as PUT /v1/messaging_providers/email; with neither, 422 (param `provider_id`). Only Atlas's own sign-in emails are sent (verification code, magic link, password reset, password changed, account exists notice, organization invitation); every subject starts with "[Atlas test] " and every message ends with a development footer; template overrides and branding are not used and custom notification templates are refused. Capped per instance per day and per recipient per hour (`limits`); over a cap a send is refused with 429 DEVELOPMENT_EMAIL_LIMIT_REACHED. The instance then counts as able to deliver email, and preflight warns `email_development_sender`. Atlas never sends with an account of its own. 201 when the mode is turned on, 200 when it already was. 409 DEVELOPMENT_EMAIL_NOT_ALLOWED on a production instance.
**Required scope:** `messaging:write`

`POST /v1/messaging_providers/email/development`

Same resolution, single use, MFA and sign-in path as POST /v1/client/migrations/better_auth/exchange, always returning the tokens in the body (or a sign_in_attempt when a second factor is owed). item.name: POST Server-to-server exchange of an old `source` session for an Atlas session, once (what migrationBridge({ source }) c

request.description:

The token is verified (vendor JWT against the bridge's issuer and keys, or sha256 matched against imported sessions), mapped to the imported user, spent in the single-use ledger and then takes the normal sign-in path (guards, MFA policy, post_login Actions, audit). Send `client_secret` to choose the secret yourself (32-256 random printable characters), so a provisioning script can re-run safely. `require_verified_email: true` makes /oauth2/authorize refuse users whose primary email is not verified. Idempotent create: `external_ref` returns the existing object on a repeat (200, `idempotent_replay: true`, no secret re-shown); `metadata` tags it (filter lists with ?metadata[key]=value). `add_redirect_origins: true` also adds the redirect URIs' origins to allowed_origins (append only; listed in added_origins); a client that a connected integration signs users in with (its oauth_client_id, or tagged metadata product=<integration id>) gets them automatically.

Works once, within 10 minutes of the POST /v1/oauth_clients or POST /v1/oauth_clients/{id}/rotate_secret that generated it, and only while that secret is still the client's current one. The secret is kept encrypted for that window only and is cleared by this call, so a second call, a call after the window, a secret you chose yourself, or one rotated away since is 410 and the answer is to rotate. Audited (oauth_client.secret_revealed / oauth_client.secret_reveal_refused). An operator token needs a recent MFA. With `?dry_run=true` nothing is consumed: the response says whether the reveal is still available and until when. Unknown client is 404.

item.name: POST Sign a user out of this app and of Atlas in one server-side call. The path takes the client id (`oac_...`) or its p

request.description:
Sign a user out of this app and of Atlas in one server-side call. The path takes the client id (`oac_...`) or its public `client_id`. Body `sid` = the `sid` claim of the id_token Atlas issued to this client. Revokes every refresh grant this client holds under the sid (offline_access included) and forgets its ID-token-only sign-in; revokes the Atlas session itself exactly like POST /v1/sessions/{id}/revoke (session.revoked webhook, back-channel logout to every other app signed in through it); and sends this client a back-channel logout so its other servers hear it. Afterwards the Atlas cookie in the browser points at a dead session, so no redirect to /oauth2/logout is needed (it remains available when you want a post_logout_redirect_uri). Needs BOTH `oauth_clients:write` and `sessions:write` on the key. 404 when the client or the session is not in this instance; 403 when that session never signed in to this client (use POST /v1/sessions/{id}/revoke for any session). A session that had already ended answers `session: "already_ended"` and still has the grants of this client under it revoked. Supports `?dry_run=true`.
**Required scope:** `oauth_clients:write`

POST Bulk-create users from an array, deduping by verified email, through the same path sign-up uses. Plaintext password

request.description:
Bulk-create users from an array, deduping by verified email, through the same path sign-up uses. Plaintext passwords are Argon2id-hashed; Argon2id, bcrypt, PBKDF2/scrypt (Django, passlib), Firebase scrypt (with password_hash_config.firebase), Better Auth scrypt and Node crypto.scrypt `scrypt$N$r$p$salt$key` hashes are imported verbatim (a Node string with an all-digit salt is also a valid Django one and must be named: password_hash_algorithm scrypt_node or scrypt_django; scrypt_node takes salt_encoding, default utf8 = the salt text as written). A hash that does not describe itself is imported by naming it: password_hash_algorithm (scrypt, pbkdf2, md5, sha1, sha256, sha512, their _salted forms, hmac_sha256, bcrypt, …) with password_hash_params (scrypt n or log_n / r / p / key_length; pbkdf2 digest / iterations / key_length; md5 and sha* salt_position prefix|suffix; encoding and salt_encoding hex|base64|base64url|utf8) and password_salt; the hash may be the bare digest or `<salt>$<hash>` / `<name>$<salt>$<hash>` (e.g. `scrypt$<salt>$<hash>` with the parameters given separately). Every imported hash is checked with a constant-time compare and upgraded to Argon2id on the first successful sign-in; a format that cannot be checked is rejected per row (unsupported_password_hash, the message names the field). Each row may also carry external_id, image_url (alias profile_image_url: an https URL; an invalid one fails the row with invalid_image_url), created_at, phone_number / phone_numbers and organization_memberships (org by id, external id or slug, plus a role); create_organizations:true creates a missing org. Per-row failures are recorded, never fatal. Body: an array of users, or { users, upsert?, notify?, create_organizations?, password_hash_config? }. An import never notifies the imported users: with notify false (the default) no email, SMS or push is sent as a consequence of the import, whatever templates are configured; notify:true is reserved for future welcome messages and currently sends nothing.
**Required scope:** `jobs:write`

`POST /v1/user_imports`

A self-describing hash (Argon2id, bcrypt, Django / passlib PBKDF2 and scrypt, Node `scrypt$N$r$p$salt$key`, Firebase scrypt, phpass, LDAP {SSHA}) is stored as given (a Node scrypt string whose salt is all digits is also a valid Django one: 400 until you name `scrypt_node` or `scrypt_django`); any other is named with `password_hash_algorithm` (scrypt, pbkdf2, md5, sha1, sha256, sha512, hmac_sha256, …) plus `password_hash_params` (e.g. scrypt { n, r, p, key_length, salt_encoding }) and `password_salt`, or as `<name>$<salt>$<hash>`; `password_hasher` is the Clerk name, used only when the hash does not describe itself. An imported hash is upgraded to Argon2id on the first successful sign-in; one Atlas cannot check is a 400 naming the field), name, profile picture (image_url, alias profile_image_url: an https URL stored as given) and metadata. item.name: authorize
GET Authorization endpoint. Exact redirect_uri match, PKCE for public clients; authenticates via the hosted session and

query.description: Must be `code` (anything else is an unsupported_response_type error).
The registered client id. Required.
Must exactly match one of the client's registered redirect URIs.
Space-delimited scopes (e.g. `openid profile email offline_access`). `organizations` adds every organization membership to the ID token and userinfo as an `orgs` claim (`[{ id, slug, role }]`).
Opaque value echoed back on the redirect.
Value bound into the id_token.
PKCE challenge (required for public clients).
PKCE method; only S256 is supported.
The API (resource server identifier) the access token is for. Alias of `resource`.
RFC 8707 resource indicator: the API the access token is for.
How the response is returned: `query` (default), `fragment`, `web_message` (popup), or a JARM `*.jwt` mode for a signed response.
RFC 9101 (JAR) signed request object carrying the parameters.
RFC 9126 PAR `urn:ietf:params:oauth:request_uri:…` from POST /oauth2/par; the lodged parameters replace the front-channel ones.
RFC 9396 Rich Authorization Request: a JSON array of typed objects.

OpenID Grant Management: `create` makes a new grant, `merge` adds this request's permissions to the grant named by `grant_id`, `replace` makes that grant exactly this request. The token response then carries the `grant_id`. A merge or replace that adds anything the grant does not already hold shows the consent screen again (`consent_required` under prompt=none); one that only keeps or drops permissions does not. Also accepted in a PAR body and in a request object.
The grant a `merge` or `replace` targets. Required with those actions, refused with `create`; an unknown, revoked or another client's or user's grant is `invalid_grant`.

Space-delimited OIDC prompt: `none` (no UI; answers login_required / consent_required / interaction_required / account_selection_required instead), `login` (always re-authenticate: the ID token then carries a fresh `auth_time`), `consent` (always show the consent screen), `select_account` (the account chooser), `create` (open the hosted sign-up screen instead of sign-in; a signed-in browser is sent to sign-up too, `create` with `none` is interaction_required).

Maximum acceptable age (seconds) of the end-user authentication, measured from the session's `auth_time`; an older session must re-authenticate. `max_age=0` always re-authenticates (same as prompt=login), so a step-up check gets an ID token whose `auth_time` is the moment the user just signed in again. Under prompt=none a stale session is login_required.

An email address: prefills the email field on the hosted sign-in and sign-up page (and is passed to your own sign-in page with a delegated login). When its domain is a VERIFIED domain of one of the instance's organizations and that organization has an active SSO connection (OIDC, SAML or WS-Federation), the browser goes straight to that identity provider and the email step is skipped. Anything that is not an email address is ignored.

A domain name (acme.com): routes to the SSO connection of the organization that verified it, like an email login_hint, without prefilling an email. Wins over the domain of login_hint. An unverified or unknown domain, or an organization without an active connection, shows the normal hosted page.

Space-separated BCP 47 tags in order of preference (also accepted as `locale`): the language of the hosted sign-in / sign-up page, consent screen and account chooser. The first supported tag wins (a regional tag such as es-MX maps to its language), narrowed by the instance's enabled locales; otherwise Accept-Language, then the instance default.

Space-separated requested authentication context classes, voluntary per OIDC: `urn:atlas:acr:basic` or `urn:atlas:acr:mfa`. The sign-in is not refused for a voluntary value; the ID token's `acr` (and `amr`) say what the session actually met, so check them. To require MFA, send it as essential in `claims`: {"id_token":{"acr":{"essential":true,"values":["urn:atlas:acr:mfa"]}}} — a sign-in that does not meet it ends with unmet_authentication_requirements.
A previously-issued id_token naming the end user the client expects.

OpenID Connect Core §5.5 claims request: a JSON object with `id_token` and/or `userinfo` members naming individual claims (null, or `{ essential, value, values }`). Honoured within what the granted scopes permit: tenant custom-scope claims are released where asked for (the standard profile and email claims come with their scopes either way); an essential `acr` the sign-in does not meet fails with `unmet_authentication_requirements`; a `sub` value must name the signed-in user; an `org_id` or `org_slug` `value`/`values` picks the organization the tokens are issued in (the first the user belongs to; when marked essential and none match, or no organization is involved, the request ends with `access_denied`). Also accepted in a PAR body and in a request object.

Organization id or slug the authorization must be made in. The signed-in user has to be a member, else the request ends with `access_denied`. The ID token, access token and userinfo then carry `org_id`, `org_slug`, `org_role` and `org_permissions` for it. Also accepted in a PAR body and in a request object.
Organization id or slug to brand the hosted sign-in page for. When the signed-in user is a member, the tokens are issued in it (org_* claims); otherwise it is ignored.
Alias of organization_hint.

An opaque value of your own (at most 512 bytes, no control characters; an invite token, a tenant hint). Carried through the hosted sign-in and sign-up pages (including prompt=create) to the user the sign-up creates, and sent to your before_user_create hook as data.request.app_context next to data.request.client_id and data.request.login_hint. Never logged in full. It comes from the browser: verify it in your hook. Longer or malformed values are refused with an error page. Also accepted in a PAR body and in a request object.
Delegated login: the single-use verifier the browser brings back from your own sign-in page (see /v1/oauth_login_requests/accept). Atlas signs the accepted user in and continues the request.

Which audience the hosted sign-in and sign-up pages theme for: a key of branding.audiences (1-32 characters: a-z, 0-9, _ and -). The page uses that audience's heading, subheading, logo and primary colour; an unknown hint shows the default branding. UI only: it is not put in any token.
Referral code (3-64 of A-Z a-z 0-9 _ -). Also read from the instance's other referral URL parameters (default via, aff).
Referral platform click id. Kept only with ref_consent=granted.
Referral platform anonymous visitor id. Kept only with ref_consent=granted.
`granted`: the app's consent manager allowed referral tracking, so the click and anonymous ids may be used. `not_required` (or absent): only the code is used.
When the referral was captured (ISO 8601). Defaults to now.
Where the client found the referral (custom, a referral program id, url, cookie). Kept for the delivery log only.
Who decided consent for the ids (app, url, a consent manager id, none). Kept for the delivery log only.

request.description:
A partner (a preset such as Cookie Munch) asks Atlas to mint it a narrow data-rights key for one instance, so the site owner never copies an instance secret key to it (`mintFrom: "atlas"`). The partner signs the request like its deliveries (Cookie Munch: `CookieMunch-Partner-Signature: t=<unix s>,kid=<key id>,ed25519=<base64url>` over `<t>.<raw body>`, key picked by `kid` from its JWKS; retired keys verify). A second valid mint for the same site rotates: the previous key is revoked. 401 with `reason` (missing_signature, malformed_signature, stale, unknown_kid, bad_signature); 403 `wrong_receiver` or `not_linked`; 404 for a partner that mints no keys; 409 `replayed`; 429; 503 when the key set or the partner cannot be reached (retry).

item.name: wstrust
POST WS-Trust 1.3 security token service (Issue, Renew, Cancel and Validate bindings, chosen by RequestType). Issue exch

query.description: Publishable key of the instance (or call on the instance host).

request.description:
WS-Trust 1.3 security token service (Issue, Renew, Cancel and Validate bindings, chosen by RequestType). Issue exchanges a username/password, an Atlas-issued SAML assertion or a proxy-vouched Kerberos principal for a signed SAML 1.1 or 2.0 assertion for a relying party that has the token service enabled: a bearer token, or a holder-of-key token bound to a certificate (PublicKey + UseKey) or to a symmetric proof key (SymmetricKey, with P_SHA1 key computation from requestor entropy). Renew issues a fresh token for an earlier one within eight hours of the first; Cancel revokes a token; Validate reports whether a token is valid.

`POST /v1/wstrust/13/issue`
